meta.title: Yoruba A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Yoruba → English (see the Yoruba, recall the meaning) and English → Yoruba (see an English meaning, recall the Yoruba). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Yoruba, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 192 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the ordinals, the times of day and meals, directions and places, clothes, work and jobs, relatives and the stages of life, feelings, travel, the countryside and the weather, the body and health, food and the kitchen, the things of a home, talking and learning, the everyday verbs of doing, describing people, and the feasts and the faith — and the other 558 are the commonest remaining words of the Yoruba Wikipedia (its articles of 150 words or more, the one-line stubs left out). About half of that Wikipedia is written with its tone marks, and the counts of the carefully marked articles decide how an unmarked spelling is shared out among the words it could be (ti, tí, tì). The corpus is encyclopaedic, which shows in the fill (government, history, sport), and the cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here, and some of the commonest are missing from it (ta ni 'who', ibo 'where', nísinsìnyí 'now', tún 'again', burú 'to be bad'). Every word is written in standard Yoruba spelling WITH ITS TONE MARKS — an acute for a high tone (á), a grave for a low one (à), no mark for a mid tone — because the tones are part of the word: ọkọ is 'husband', ọkọ̀ 'vehicle', ọkọ́ 'hoe'. The Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters and the marks. One spelling is often several words (dá 'to create', 'to stop', 'to break'); the card is the spelling and gives the first meaning of each. Many Yoruba adjectives are verbs ('to be big', 'to be good'), and are taught as Wiktionary gives them. Example sentences are few: 197 of the 750 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 60 Yoruba sentences with a translation; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Yoruba voice, and one without it would read the word in another language's sounds. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, spellings and tone marks: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Yoruba Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
